title: Time
subtitle: era, spell, phase; in time and on time
summary: Learn the nouns English uses for different periods of time, the fixed expressions with time, and the verbs and adjectives that describe how time passes.

lesson.heading: Periods of time
rows: a major historical or geological period
the Ice Age, the Stone Age, the Middle Ages, the computer age
a long period, perhaps several decades
After the war, a new era of stability began.
a stretch of time of a stated length
a spell of hot weather; he's had a couple of spells in hospital
a period of development, or a particular point in a process
The city went through several stages of development.
a period which is part of a longer period; can also mean stage
Most teenagers go through a phase of being lazy.

lesson.heading: Age, era and spell in use
lesson.text: **Age** and **era** are both long, but *age* usually names a whole historical or technological epoch, while *era* is a stretch of history with a particular character. A **spell** is short and rather vague.

examples.text: The last two decades of the twentieth century saw the beginning of the computer **age**.
These factories mark the beginning of a new **era** of industrial development for the country.
We had a very cold **spell** in February. All the water pipes froze up.
My son went through a **phase** of not wanting to go to school when he was about nine or ten.

lesson.heading: Useful expressions with time
rows: many times; very emphatic and usually negative
used about long periods of time

lesson.heading: These expressions in use
lesson.text: Note that **by the time** is followed by a present tense, not by *will*.

examples.text: During the 1980s I lived in Barcelona **for a time**.
The doctor says you should stay in bed **for the time being**.
She can get a bit bad-tempered **at times**.
**By the time** we get home this pizza will be cold!
examples.wrong: By the time we will get home

examples.text: I've told you **time and time again** not to ring me at the office!

left.label: in time
left.text: at the right time, or with enough time to do something
examples: We got there just **in time** for dinner.
We arrived just **in time** to hear the Prime Minister's speech.
Hi! You're just **in time** for coffee.

right.label: on time
examples: Our plane was **on time** and she was waiting for us at the airport.
I expect she will be late - the trains are never **on time**.
I'll do my best to be **on time** for the meeting.

lesson.heading: Verbs for time passing
rows: pass (formal; normally in the perfect or past, without adverbs)
Ten years had elapsed since they last saw each other.
Time seems to fly as you get older.
continue for a stated length of time
This film lasts for three hours.
The meeting went on for two hours.
continue tediously - stronger than go on
The meeting dragged on for two hours.

lesson.heading: Adjectives describing duration
lesson.text: These adjectives say how long something lasts - usually not very long at all.

examples.text: There was a **momentary** loss of electrical power and the data was lost.
I just got a **fleeting** glimpse of the President as his car drove past.

examples.note: timeless = never seeming old or out of date

lesson.text: Remember the difference: *We arrived in time for the film* (early enough) but *The film started on time* (punctually).

exercises.prompt: The Minister said that before the new law came into force there would be a ___ of six months when people could hand in firearms.
exercises.explanation: Period is used for a stretch of time of a stated length.

exercises.prompt: We had a very cold ___ in February. All the water pipes froze up.
exercises.explanation: A spell is an indefinite but short period, often used for weather and illness.

exercises.prompt: The archaeologists discovered some tools which dated from the Stone ___.
exercises.explanation: Age names major historical or geological periods: the Ice Age, the Stone Age.

exercises.prompt: The new university will be built in three ___, beginning with the science faculty.
exercises.explanation: A stage is a period of development or a particular point in a process; phases is also possible here.

exercises.prompt: Over the ___ of a century, from 1900 to 2000, the population grew steadily.
exercises.explanation: Over the course of time / over the course of the last century is used for long periods.

exercises.prompt: Time seems to ___ when you're enjoying yourself.
exercises.explanation: Time flies means it passes very quickly.

exercises.prompt: A period of seven years ___ between the two earthquakes.
exercises.explanation: Elapse is a formal verb for time passing, normally used in the past or perfect.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with the adjective or verb that completes it.

pairs.left: Shakespeare's plays never grow old; they have a ___ quality.
She only stayed for about ten minutes - it was just a ___ visit.
There was a ___ pause, then the official said she would help.
The lecture ___ for almost three hours and everyone was bored.

exercises.prompt: You want to say that the weather in your city can be very hot occasionally. Which expression do you use?
exercises.explanation: At times means occasionally, now and then.

exercises.statement: 'Our plane was in time, so we weren't late' uses the right expression.
exercises.explanation: On time means punctual: Our plane was on time, so we weren't late.

exercises.statement: 'By the time you get this card, I'll be in New York' is correct English.
exercises.explanation: Correct - by the time is followed by a present tense, not by will.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to tell a child off for something they have done often.
exercises.answer: I've told you time and time again not to leave the fridge door open!
exercises.explanation: Time and time again is very emphatic and usually appears in negative contexts.

exercises.prompt: Does each expression mean 'often' or 'not often / only for now'?
